strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating multimodal agents that must combine visual interpretation with long-horizon web search rather than merely recognize a salient entity.

The 311-item benchmark covers eight domains and is intentionally challenging; the large gap between no-search, image-search, and full-rollout performance provides useful evidence that retrieval and iterative tool use matter.
Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation is an intuitive curation principle for constructing questions whose answers are not directly visible in the input image.
The evaluation includes proprietary and open-weight models, category and difficulty breakdowns, trajectory statistics, and a manually constructed error taxonomy with illustrative cases.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and its motivating examples clearly communicate the intended task.
weaknesses: The central claim that the benchmark specifically measures sustained, fine-grained multimodal reasoning is not convincingly validated. There is no text-only browsing-agent control, image-ablation study, source-oracle experiment, or comparison against simpler reverse-image-search pipelines. Low accuracy alone does not establish that visual reasoning, rather than retrieval difficulty or pipeline failures, is the bottleneck.

Cropping, localized grounding, and provenance verification are repeatedly presented as defining contributions, but cropping is excluded from the main experiments, provenance is not directly scored, and no bounding-box results are reported despite the abstract claiming an assessment of bounding-box production and cropped-image search.

The baseline suite is incomplete. GPT-5 has no full-rollout result, only one open-weight model is evaluated, and relevant browsing systems or task-specific agents are not compared. This limits conclusions about both benchmark difficulty and the proposed framework.

Dataset validation is insufficiently documented. The paper provides no human baseline, inter-annotator agreement, ambiguity analysis, per-item source verification protocol, or substantive audit demonstrating that questions remain answerable as the web changes. The claim of complete human–LLM-judge agreement lacks a sample size and evaluation procedure.

Reproducibility is weak: prompts, model snapshot details, decoding settings, webpage summarization procedure, cached retrieval artifacts, tool schemas, acceptable-answer construction, and planned dataset/code availability are not adequately specified. The project-page field is blank, and reliance on proprietary SerpApi results and a Gemini summarizer further complicates replication.

The evaluation pipeline introduces serious confounds. Retrieved pages are summarized by another MLLM, so measured performance combines the tested agent with an inadequately characterized summarizer. Qwen also produces 421 invalid calls on 45 tasks, meaning its low rollout score partly measures framework compatibility rather than browsing ability.

The difficulty split is circular because it is defined retrospectively using performance by o3 and Gemini, then used to analyze those models. Adversarial filtering with several evaluated model families can likewise induce model-specific selection bias.

Several empirical claims are overstated or inconsistent. Qwen full-rollout accuracy is 6.1% in Table 1 but 6.9% in the abstract and conclusion. The eight primary categories are described as approximately balanced despite substantially different apparent sample sizes, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for small category subsets.

Novelty relative to concurrent MM-BrowseComp and BrowseComp-VL is argued mostly qualitatively. Cross-benchmark experiments or systematic measurements of localized visual dependence and reasoning-chain length are needed to substantiate the claimed distinction.

The collection of images and frames from YouTube, Bilibili, and papers raises copyright, privacy, licensing, and redistribution questions that are not adequately addressed; the manuscript's unclear statement that keyframes underwent 'deanoymouization' for sensitive content compounds this concern.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating agents that must combine visual understanding with open-web information seeking.
The 311 tasks span eight domains, and the spatial/temporal extrapolation framing is an intuitive curation heuristic for asking questions whose answers are not directly visible.
The evaluation includes several strong proprietary and open-weight models, no-search/image-search/full-rollout conditions, category breakdowns, trajectory statistics, and qualitative failure cases.
The low absolute performance suggests that the collected tasks are challenging and may provide useful diagnostic examples.
weaknesses: The central claim of sustained, fine-grained multimodal reasoning is not demonstrated. There is no image-removal, text-only browsing, oracle-event, or controlled visual-cue ablation. In the reported o3 rollouts, only 75 of 1,688 search calls are image searches, with median image-search usage equal to zero; cropping—the mechanism emphasized for localized visual reasoning—is omitted from the main experiments. The benchmark may therefore mostly measure initial visual identification followed by text search.

Dataset construction and quality control are insufficiently documented. The paper omits annotator counts, instructions, agreement, answer/source verification procedures, task-level provenance, ambiguity checks, and a completed human baseline. It consequently does not establish that all questions are uniquely answerable or that 311 items adequately support the broad claims.

The evaluation pipeline introduces major confounds. Gemini-generated summaries are cached and supplied to every model, potentially biasing comparisons and hiding retrieval or visual-processing failures. Qwen receives half the rollout budget and produces 421 invalid calls on 45 tasks, so its score reflects framework incompatibility as well as capability. GPT-5 is not evaluated in full-rollout mode despite being presented as a principal frontier baseline.

Relevant agent baselines such as MMSearch-R1, WebWatcher/BrowseComp-VL systems, or other established browsing agents are not run on the benchmark. Conversely, the proposed agents are not tested on prior benchmarks. Thus, claims of preserving BrowseComp's difficulty profile and improving upon the evaluation coverage of related benchmarks are unsupported by direct comparisons.

Statistical reporting is weak: there are no confidence intervals, repeated runs, significance tests, cost or latency comparisons, or robustness analyses for changing web results. The claim that cached search results remain stable is asserted without measurement.

The Easy/Hard partition is defined retrospectively using success by the same evaluated models, making the split circular and rendering several observations—such as zero no-search accuracy on the Hard subset—largely tautological.

Evaluation reliability is not adequately substantiated. The paper reports 'complete agreement' between humans and an LLM judge without giving the sample size, sampling procedure, rubric, or agreement statistic. Error analysis uses a single author-assigned dominant label without reliability checks, and the main text attributes the distribution to Gemini on the current dataset while the appendix describes it as an o3 pilot on a previous dataset.

There are consequential internal inconsistencies: Qwen full-rollout accuracy is 6.1% in Table 1 but 6.9% in the abstract and conclusion; the appendix's human row is blank; and some appendix analyses are ambiguously tied to different models or dataset versions.

Reproducibility is poor. The project-page field is empty, and essential prompts, agent-policy details, summarization templates, acceptable-answer sets, cached retrieval artifacts, and release commitments are absent.

The novelty over MM-BrowseComp and BrowseComp-VL appears incremental: Spatial–Temporal Extrapolation is primarily a descriptive data-curation recipe rather than a validated methodological advance. The paper does not empirically isolate what its proposed construction contributes.

The manuscript does not meaningfully address privacy, copyright, consent, or licensing for screenshots and frames collected from YouTube, Bilibili, papers, and other web sources. The vague statement about processing sensitive content is not an adequate ethical or data-governance discussion.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and important gap: existing multimodal browsing benchmarks may be solvable through entity matching or nearby text rather than sustained visual reasoning. The motivation is clear and well positioned relative to MMSearch, BrowseComp, BrowseComp-VL, and MM-BrowseComp.

MMSearch-Plus contains 311 tasks across eight reasonably diverse domains, and the spatial-temporal extrapolation principle is an intuitive, useful recipe for constructing questions whose answers are not directly visible in the prompt image.

The evaluation covers several strong closed and open multimodal models under no-search, image-search, and iterative-search conditions. The large gain for o3 from 15.1% to 36.0% provides concrete evidence that browsing matters while leaving substantial headroom.

Category-level results, trajectory statistics, and qualitative error cases provide useful diagnostic information. The finding that additional retrieval can hurt Qwen highlights an important challenge in integrating perception, retrieval, and long-horizon planning.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and candid about limitations such as retrieval failures, invalid tool calls, and the absence of video support.
weaknesses: The central claim that the benchmark requires sustained fine-grained multimodal reasoning is not convincingly isolated. There is no text-only agent with image-derived metadata, image-removal or masking ablation, oracle visual-description baseline, or comparable control showing that performance cannot largely arise from textual retrieval after an initial visual cue. Indeed, the reported o3 trajectories use only 75 image-search calls versus 1,613 text-search calls.

Cropping and localized visual grounding are central to the motivation, yet cropping is omitted from the main experiments because it reportedly hurts performance. No quantitative crop-tool results, bounding-box evaluation, or systematic visual-cue ablation is provided, despite the abstract suggesting that bounding-box production and cropped-image search are assessed.

Benchmark validity is insufficiently documented. The paper lacks a human baseline, a systematic solvability and ambiguity audit, inter-annotator agreement, detailed answer/source verification procedures, and analysis of how many questions depend on inaccessible video narration or volatile web content. Difficulty labels are also defined retrospectively using the same model results being analyzed.

The evaluation contains consequential confounds: Gemini summarizes image-search results for every evaluated model; Qwen receives only 10 search rounds while other models receive 20; models differ substantially in tool-call reliability; and GPT-5 lacks a full-rollout result. These choices weaken both fairness and conclusions about model capabilities.

Reproducibility is presently limited. The project-page field is blank, dataset and code availability are unclear, and important details such as complete prompts, decoding settings, repeated-run variance, API versions, and cached retrieval artifacts are not reported. Caching only image-search results does not address the volatility of text search and webpages.

There are notable internal inconsistencies: Qwen full-rollout accuracy is 6.1% in the main table but 6.9% in the abstract and conclusion, while the error-analysis description alternately attributes annotations to Gemini on the current benchmark and to o3 on a previous approximately 300-item version. These discrepancies reduce confidence in the empirical record.

The 311-item scale leads to small per-category subsets and potentially high uncertainty, but no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. Several interpretations of small category-level differences are therefore too strong.

The data are drawn from YouTube, Bilibili, papers, and other public web sources, but the manuscript provides no substantive discussion of copyright, licensing, consent, privacy, or redistribution policy. Overall, the benchmark idea is promising, but the missing validity controls and evaluation confounds leave the main claim slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: evaluating agents that must combine visual inspection with iterative open-web search.
The spatial-temporal extrapolation idea is intuitive and produces challenging questions whose answers are not necessarily visible in the supplied frame.

The benchmark spans eight domains, and the evaluation includes several frontier proprietary models, a strong open model, multiple tool configurations, category breakdowns, and qualitative trajectory analysis.
The paper is generally clear and includes useful analyses of tool transitions, retrieval failures, and differences between OCR-plus-text-search and region-based image search.
The low absolute accuracies and documented failure cases suggest that the tasks expose genuine limitations of current browsing agents.
weaknesses: The central claim that the benchmark enforces fine-grained multimodal reasoning is not adequately validated. There is no question-only, shuffled-image, masked-region, OCR-only, or image-description baseline. Moreover, o3 with text search achieves 37.0%, exceeding full rollout and nearly matching the best SoM result, so the experiments do not isolate the contribution of visual evidence.

The SoM experiment is substantially confounded: human annotators provide task-specific, verified boxes around key entities, and the SoM condition also introduces cropping and sub-image-search capabilities. Thus, the small gains cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed representation or to autonomous visual grounding. No automatic-region baseline or oracle-cost analysis is provided.

Reported improvements are small and lack repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. With only 311 tasks and much smaller category subsets, changes of 1–4 accuracy points may represent only a handful of examples. The abstract is also inconsistent with Table 1: it calls 36.0% the strongest end-to-end accuracy although the table reports 37.6%.

Benchmark construction and quality control are insufficiently documented. The paper does not report annotator counts, agreement, answer-verification procedures, task rejection rates, or independent solvability checks. Human browser accuracy is only 22.8% under a restrictive 10–20 minute limit, raising concerns about ambiguity, inaccessible evidence, or unrealistic search difficulty.

The Easy and lite splits are circular and model-dependent. Easy is defined using success by o3 or Gemini, while the lite split removes every item answered without search by the evaluated models; consequently, the reported zero-shot results and some split-level conclusions follow directly from construction rather than providing independent evidence.

Evaluation is not fully controlled or model-agnostic: Gemini generates task-conditioned summaries of search results for all evaluated agents, potentially injecting its own reasoning and creating unequal dependencies. Search budgets also differ for Qwen, several baseline cells are missing, and caching task-conditioned summaries per image is insufficiently explained when images or question formulations repeat.

Despite emphasizing provenance-aware search, the primary metric judges only final-answer accuracy. Citation correctness, source quality, evidence entailment, and provenance completeness are not evaluated. The claimed complete human agreement with the LLM judge is unsupported by a reported sample size or protocol.

Reproducibility is limited for a dynamic web benchmark: only 30 examples are included in the supplementary material, while search dates, complete API/model settings, stochastic decoding details, repeated trials, and snapshots of retrieved evidence are not sufficiently specified. Claims that screenshots are absent from training data because direct image search fails are also unjustified.

The comparison to humans and claims about comparative advantages are not reliable without annotator population details, per-task verification, matched tools, or uncertainty estimates. Ethical and licensing statements similarly assert compliance for public platform content without item-level license documentation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating agents that must combine fine-grained visual inspection with iterative web search.
Spatial–Temporal Extrapolation is an intuitive task-design principle, and the benchmark covers eight reasonably diverse domains with difficult, short-answer questions.
The evaluation includes several frontier closed-source models and an open-source model under multiple tool configurations.
The trajectory, tool-transition, and error analyses provide useful descriptive evidence about current agents’ search behavior.
weaknesses: The central claim that the benchmark specifically measures genuine multimodal browsing is not convincingly established. The strongest o3 result uses the text-search-only tool condition (37.0%), outperforming full multimodal rollout (36.0%); on MMSearch-Plus-lite it also exceeds full rollout plus SoM (31.4% versus 30.1%). Missing image-removal, image-shuffling, oracle-cue, and modality-dependency tests make it unclear how many tasks truly require the claimed visual search behavior.

The SoM contribution relies on privileged, human-curated bounding boxes rather than agent-generated localization. Its net gains are only 1.0–3.9 percentage points on 311 tasks, with no confidence intervals, paired significance tests, repeated runs, or accounting for regressions. This is insufficient evidence for a robust method contribution.

Benchmark construction and validation are under-specified: annotator count and expertise, annotation protocol, ground-truth sourcing, answer verification, deduplication, quality-control agreement, and task rejection rates are not reported. Assertions that screenshots are absent from training data or cannot be found through direct image search are not substantiated.

The evaluation pipeline is difficult to reproduce and potentially confounded. Live SerpAPI results are time-varying, webpages and image results are summarized by Gemini, caches are created per benchmark image, and there is no analysis of summarizer errors, search variance, or run-to-run stability.

The human baseline is not credible enough to anchor difficulty: humans score only 22.8%, substantially below o3, despite receiving 10–20 minutes with a browser. The paper omits the number of annotators, assignment counts, training, success criteria, and adjudication, so this result may reflect the evaluation procedure rather than task difficulty.

Answer accuracy is determined by GPT-4o, but the claimed complete human agreement lacks a sample size, sampling procedure, rubric, and agreement statistic. More importantly, the paper calls the benchmark provenance-aware without evaluating citation correctness, evidence sufficiency, or provenance at all.

The lite split is selected using the same tested models whose performance is then reported, making its zero no-search scores true by construction and introducing selection circularity. Difficulty labels are similarly model-dependent and likely to drift.

Reproducibility is limited because only 30 examples are supplied with the submission, while the full 311-task benchmark, annotations, acceptable-answer sets, human-curated boxes, cached retrievals, and complete evaluation artifacts are not demonstrably available. Regularly refreshing tasks would further undermine stable longitudinal comparison.

Ethical and licensing treatment is too general for screenshots taken from public videos and papers: public accessibility does not itself imply redistribution rights or consent, and the paper provides no item-level license audit or concrete takedown procedure.

There are notable reporting and presentation problems: the abstract says the strongest system scores 36.0% although Table 1 reports 37.6%; several claims overstate what the evidence supports; and appendix trajectories contain placeholder-like redactions such as “russian-1,” weakening clarity. strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: evaluating browsing agents that must combine localized visual evidence with iterative web search rather than relying on a single reverse-image-search result.
The spatial-temporal extrapolation principle is intuitive and produces diverse, challenging tasks involving facts beyond the depicted frame or moment.

The evaluation covers several frontier closed-source models, a strong open-source model, multiple search configurations, and a human baseline. The trajectory, tool-transition, category-level, and failure analyses provide useful empirical insight.
The paper is clearly written and well illustrated, and it discusses privacy, benchmark drift, limitations, and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that the benchmark specifically measures necessary fine-grained multimodal browsing is not decisively validated. Important controls are missing, including question-only, OCR/caption-plus-text-search, shuffled-image, oracle-region, and unimodal-agent baselines. Moreover, o3's text-search configuration matches or exceeds full multimodal rollout overall, including 31.4% versus 30.1% on MMSearch-Plus-lite.

Dataset validity needs stronger evidence. There are only 311 tasks, the reported 22.8% human accuracy is unusually low, and the paper does not provide a sufficiently detailed expert solvability audit, ambiguity analysis, inter-annotator agreement, or per-task provenance validation. These omissions make it difficult to distinguish agent difficulty from underspecification or inaccessible web evidence.

The SoM intervention relies on human-curated, human-verified bounding boxes, effectively supplying oracle localization. Its practical significance as an agent module is therefore limited, and the small aggregate gains are reported without confidence intervals, paired significance tests, repeated runs, or an automatic-box baseline. Large numbers of newly correct cases alongside small net gains also imply substantial regressions that are not analyzed.

Model comparisons are confounded because Gemini summarizes retrieved pages and image-search results for every evaluated agent. Search depth also differs for Qwen. Consequently, the results do not cleanly isolate each model's browsing ability or establish a fully open-source baseline.

Reproducibility is limited by live SerpAPI results, cached model-generated summaries, unclear release coverage beyond the 30 supplementary examples, and incomplete reporting of retrieval snapshots and evaluation variance. The LLM-judge validation also lacks a stated sample size and detailed protocol.

Difficulty labels and the lite subset are defined using the same models later evaluated, creating circularity and model-specific selection bias. Regularly refreshing the benchmark may address contamination but weakens longitudinal comparability. The relation to concurrent multimodal browsing benchmarks is meaningful but incremental, so stronger validation is needed to justify acceptance.
